query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, high-temperature resistant oxide nanolaminate coating improves the surface stability of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy so that its creep and corrosion performance under extreme aerospace conditions is enhanced without compromising its favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, uniform lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (sub-micron), conformal nanolaminate coating composed of alternating layers of Al2O3 and TiO2 by atomic layer deposition (ALD).
generation.conditions: Test under simulated aerospace operating conditions including cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations, prolonged mechanical loading inducing room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, adherent nanolaminate coating that acts as a protective barrier at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The coating limits environmental attack (e.g., oxidation and corrosion) and suppresses surface-initiated creep by impeding dislocation mobility and inhibiting deleterious chemical reactions at the interface, thereby preserving the bulk’s strength–ductility balance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance and reduced room-temperature creep—reflected in lower strain rates and delayed failure—compared to the uncoated alloy, while overall mechanical strength and ductility are maintained.
generation.baseline: Performance data from the uncoated AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to be valid for aerospace fasteners where the part dimensions allow a uniformly deposited sub-micron coating; the benefits may diminish if the coating is too thick (introducing brittleness) or if the coating’s adhesion is compromised under aggressive thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in creep delay and corrosion resistance and the long-term durability of the coating under cyclic temperature and mechanical load require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy: one group with the ALD-deposited Al2O3/TiO2 nanolaminate coating and one uncoated control. Subject both groups to accelerated corrosion tests (e.g., salt spray or immersion tests), cyclic thermal shock tests simulating aerospace temperature fluctuations, and constant-load creep tests at room temperature. Monitor performance over time.
measurements: Corrosion rate (weight loss, surface pitting analysis via SEM/EDS)
Creep strain rate (using extensometry or digital image correlation during constant load testing)
Coating integrity (via cross-sectional TEM/SEM imaging before and after testing)
Mechanical properties (tensile tests to check for any reduction in strength/ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples fail to demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance and exhibit no reduction in room-temperature creep strain rate compared to uncoated controls, or if the coating exhibits degradation (e.g., debonding, cracking) that negatively impacts the mechanical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.
